For snacks and tea, they can head to the canteen, open from 8 am to 10 pm. Water coolers are placed at three locations and power cuts are taken care of by a large generator. "We get water around the clock, electricity, clean toilets and other facilities," said Constable Suresh Kumar Vats, who has been posted here for about 18 months (he is also reader to the SHO). At the back of the main building, about 20 rooms, declared 'unsafe' some time ago, are under use again, although maintenance work is still on in this portion of the building.

Meanwhile, work continues at a steady clip. Two officers — one male and one female — are stationed at the reception to listen to complaints. Most are relatively minor. The SHO of the thana, Ram Kumar, said, "The Daryaganj police station does not get many cases of serious crime. We receive about 600 cases a year, including cheating and theft, but heinous crimes are not a frequent occurrence in the area". And even though the station, like most others across the country, is somewhat short-staffed, a good percentage of the cases filed here get solved. Officials added that new recruits in the Central District are usually posted at the Daryaganj police station to help them learn the ropes of policing. Many, it is likely, do not look forward to transfers elsewhere.

Heading: Ludhiana village values its girl child - Indian Express
Content:
The lynching of Italian firm Graziano's CEO L K Chaudhary by a mob of dismissed employees has brought to the fore the poor law and order situation in western UP that corporate heads in the area have long learnt to live with. The sugar industry, the only major industry in the area, has been struggling, with three top executives of the mills killed in the recent past. Now, the executives have learnt to defend themselves.

While some have procured arms licences, others rely on private armed guards to ensure their safety in UP's 'wild west' where instances of settling scores at gun point are rampant. Carrying a gun is a necessity in the face of rampant lawlessness. "I got it when I got posted here," a chief executive of a sugar mill said.

Sugar mill officials are wary of speaking on record as it is a sensitive matter. Renowned security company Group 4 Securitas has been engaged in some sugar mills in the region. However, demands to the Government for special security cover for an industry which forms the backbone of the state economy have fallen on deaf ears. Executives still indicate their preference for police protection and are willing to pay generously for the service. "We are ready to pay charges for the police gunners," one of them told The Indian Express.

The need for enhanced security is obvious in the face of the murders of senior executives of the industry in broad daylight by the local mafia. Siddarth Upadhyay, Senior DGM, Bajaj Hindustan Group was gunned down in April, while Subhash Chand Jaggi, VP, Triveni group, was killed in 1999. SBEC sugar mill DGM (Engineering) J K Chopra was shot dead four years ago.

Sugar mill executives claim the murders took place because these individuals refused to succumb to pressures from the local mafia and politicians and refused to give them contracts running into crores.

According to IG Police (Meerut Zone) Gurdarshan Singh, a Deputy SP has been posted as Industry Relations Officer in Noida and Greater Noida. Police helplines and Quick Response Teams armed with video cameras and riot equipment have also been set up. Singh, however, said there is no blanket security cover plan for the sugar sector.

Heading: Ramadoss on ground zero, aims higher - Indian Express
Content:
Even as Punjab has the dubious distinction of having one of the lowest sex ratios in the country, a village in Ludhiana district has proved to be a remarkable exception. The average sex ratio in Bijlipur over the last six years has been recorded at 1800:1000, as opposed to Punjab's overall sex ratio of 874 females per 1000 males according to the last census.

In the period between April 2002- March 2008, the village has seen the birth of 32 girls and 17 boys. In addition, the village currently has 32 girls between the ages of 3-6 years. "This is a noteworthy achievement. A special report is being sent to the higher authorities," said multi purpose health officer, Jasbir Singh. Surinder Kaur, the local Anganwadi worker revealed that not a single case of female foeticide had been reported from this village and attributes it to the high emphasis laid on education. "The village has only one school. But the people are concerned about the education of the child. The girls cycle down to the school in the nearby town of Samrala".

Sarpanch Charanjit Singh informed The Indian Express that 70 per cent of the village's population has passed high school. Citing his personal example he said, "I have four sisters. All of them have a post graduate degree and are happily settled." Former panchayat member, Jasbir Kaur encapsulates it effectively when she says, "It is better to have five girls rather than a drug addict son. Spoilt sons inevitably take the household to doom".

Heading: Plant fate on table as CM, Tata meet - Indian Express
Content:
Union Health Minister Anbumani Ramadoss celebrated his big day on Thursday distributing pamphlets highlighting the ban to passengers at a bus terminus in Chennai. And he isn't done yet — his next big wish is a bar on all tobacco products. Ramadoss assured he wouldn't do it immediately but "take into consideration farmers", provide them "alternative employment". "My intention and my aim is to make India a tobacoo-free nation," he said. "But I do not have the power to do so."

Shah Rukh's 'happy', says next hang smokers

Minister Ramadoss and he may have traded enough fire over smoke, but on Thursday, actor Shah Rukh Khan wasn't puffing or panting. Tongue firmly in cheek, he said: "The ban is a good step to make sure that the country is smoke-free. Better step would be to ban cigarettes, make them illegal and hang anyone who is smoking. We cannot do that as we are a democratic country." Khan added: "I hope everyone calls upon their good selves to give up smoking." For Ramadoss, he added more: "I myself would try my best."

Mumbai says bye with cheer, but tomorrow another day

Mumbai bars clocked midnight on Wednesday by asking customers to stop smoking. At Bandra's famous Toto's Garage, they were rather cheerful about it, even doing a countdown to the last minutes of free smoking, and then collectively stubbing out. A nervous management, however, was unsure how long the cheer would last. While officials took it easy — October 2 being a public holiday — the story was the same as other Mumbai big joints and hotels took it upon themselves to impose the ban; ashtrays for one couldn't be seen in hotel lobbies. However, police officials acknowledged they remained clueless about their role.

Pune tries to find its way around in ban haze

In Pune, they were figuring out what fell and what didn't in the ban zone. Kashinath Telange, Controller at the Pune Municipal Corporation, had his lines drawn: "Smoking inside a bus is already banned. With the new law in place, we will ask a commuter to get down if he refuses to stop smoking." However, he wasn't as sure about fines. "We have no orders on fines as yet, but we will be receiving them soon." Pune Station Manager J M Laturkar insisted they hadn't found anyone smoking in the station. "The official directive is to impose a fine on anyone found smoking on the platform or anywhere inside the railway station," he said.

23 fined in Gujarat, ask: Is there a ban?

Gujarat had it all worked out — an orientation programme as well as proper authorisations to designated authorities to issue challans — but spent the first day ruing lack of "an enforcement squad". Health Minister Jay Narayan Vyas took a more optimistic view: it is the message rather than the enforcement itself which is important, he said. In Vadodara, the police faced no such dilemmas as 23 habitual smokers found smoking in public places were fined Rs 200 each. Many claimed they had no idea a ban existed.

Just wait till next week, warn Chennai police

In Chennai, with Minister Ramadoss around, nobody was hauled up on the first day of the ban for lighting up. But police said that was deliberate. For the first few days, it would be only warning and educating, they said. From next week onwards, stringent steps would be taken.

Heading: 13 yrs ago a small club lit the spark, Kerala village stubbed out - Indian Express
Content:
In a last ditch effort Chief Minister Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee will try to convince Tata Sons' chairman Ratan Tata of every possible help and request him to resume work at the Nano car plant in Singur during their meeting in Kolkata on Friday.

Work had been suspended at the factory from August 29 following a dharna by the Trinamool Congress outside the plant.

The meeting between the two is likely to be held at Writers' Buildings and the stakes involved for both are high, said senior government officials. The fate of the plant is to be decided in this crucial meet, which would also be attended by Minister for Commerce and Industries Nirupam Sen among others.

Even though the state Government had said elaborate security arrangements would be made once the Tatas resume work, the latter made it clear that they would not run the factory with police protection.

While former India captain Saurav Ganguly has written to Ratan Tata requesting him to resume work at the plant, Governor Gopalkrishna Gandhi said he was hopeful of a solution to the Singur imbroglio.

"Like the Prime Minister I am also hopeful of a solution for Singur," the Governor said at Gandhighat in Barrackpur on Thursday.

The state Cabinet last week issued a statement requesting the Tatas not to shift their plant elsewhere. It also requested the Opposition to accept the compensation package announced by the state Government.

The Government had said it is willing to arrange for 70 acres land from within the project area and an additional 50 per cent compensation amount to the affected farmers. However, all came to nothing, with Mamata Banerjee continuing to stick to her demand of returning 300 acres of land from within the project area and 100 acres from outside.

A section of the CPI(M) leadership is also peeved at Tata's threat to withdraw from the state. "How can they leave after going so far with the project," asked party MP Hannan Mollah.

"The Government so far had adopted a soft approach while dealing with agitators. The Durgapur Expressway was blocked for 20 days, employees working at the plant had been beaten up. Now the Government will act tough. And that is what the CM will tell the Tatas," a senior Minister told The Indian Express.

Heading: Cong adds insult to injury, to field ex-SP MLAs in MP - Indian Express
Content:
As the rest of the country braced itself for the smoking ban, which started today, it could look for some tips to a village in Kerala, which successfully stubbed tobacco out 13 years ago.

Koolimadu, 25 km from Kozhikode in north Kerala, was declared tobacco free on January 11, 1995, after a year-long campaign that managed to rope in all sections of society.

The spark to ban tobacco was lit in a small local club, Akshara, in early 1994. During a routine meeting, a member lit up a cigar. The others present immediately protested, and with tempers running high, club office-bears slapped a ban on smoking on Akshara premises. Soon, another member suggested, "Why can't we make the entire village tobacco free?"

That suggestion found many takers in the club, marking the beginning of a novel mission at the village, under the Chathamangalam gram panchayat.

Akshara took the initiative to tell the villagers about the evil s of pan masala and smoking. "We held a door-to-door campaign, distributed pamphlets and roped in doctors to conduct classes," says club spokesperson Abdul Majeed.

With several middle-aged chain smokers at Koolimadu dying of lung diseases and oral cancer in the early 90s, their call for a ban found many takers. The club members claim they weaned away many who were at a risk of contracting smoking-related diseases.

Soon local traders agreed to join the campaign, Majeed says, and they haven't looked back since.

However, he admits, the going hasn't been easy. "We have to guard against the danger of addicts relapsing to their old ways. At the same time, the younger generation has to be checked," Majeed says. Then there are new visitors who have to be told about Koolimadu's unofficial ban on tobacco. The bus junction sports several banners and boards telling first-time visitors about the same.

Some results of the blanket ban may be visible on the health front. "Earlier, Koolimadu reported cases of respiratory inflammation, bronchitis and asthma. Due to passive smoking, even children were affected. Now such cases have become rarer," claims Dr K Alikkutty, a resident of Koolimadu since 1988.

Heading: PM calls for rigorous evaluation of NREGS programmes - Indian Express
Content:
The Congress party is all set to field four Samajwadi Party MLAs from Madhya Pradesh, unaffected by the allegations that it poached them.

The resignations of these MLAs had become a sticking point between the parties because the 'poaching' took place when they were engaged in negotiating a tie-up in the Assembly and general election.

Party sources told The Indian Express that Krishna Kumar Singh (Gopadbanas), Vikram Singh alias Natiraja (Chhatarpur), Vanshmani Prasad Varma (Singrauli) and, Arjun Palia (Piparia) who resigned last month, would get tickets along with the sitting Congress MLAs.

"Definitely!" Singh replied when asked whether he was promised a ticket.

When the quartet resigned, the SP had accused the Congress of stabbing it in the back. At the national level, too, the party had a tough time defending it because there were clear indications that they would join the Congress.

Though the tickets are yet to be announced, the quartet will have it easy because the Congress thinks they are strong candidates and have sure chances of winning. In fact, they sound more certain than the Congress contenders.

Incidentally, they were all with the Congress before and had resigned when denied tickets. They had won despite changing their party affiliations just ahead of elections.

"We were as good as Independents because the SP had no base in Madhya Pradesh," Singh said, adding its future in Madhya Pradesh was bleak. The party managed to win seven tickets in 2003 and added one more to its kitty in Lanji by-election.

A Congress leader said opposing the new entrants was a futile exercise as the high command had made up its mind to give them tickets. Even the SP's state unit seems to have reconciled to the loss of four MLAs, half its strength in the state Assembly, and with the fact that the Congress will field them no matter what.

"Jo ho gaya so ho gaya," (let bygones be bygones) said Narayan Tripati, who had rushed to Delhi in the wake of the resignations to brief Mulayam Singh and Amar Singh, and was openly critical of the Congress. "If the Congress denies them tickets, the BJP would gain by wooing them," he said explaining why he had come to grips with the loss of four MLAs. Tripathi said the high command had already denied any possibility of a tie-up between the two parties in the Assembly elections.

Heading: Broadcasters’ body begins work, to act as watchdog - Indian Express
Content:
Taking note of the continuing poor performance by some states in the implementation of the National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (NREGS), Prime Minister Manmohan Singh on Thursday called upon all states to emulate the progressive ones and put in place a mechanism to rigorously evaluate the programme.

"Some states have shown good results. Some are lagging behind. I urge the states that have been behind to make all efforts to catch up with the more progressive ones," he said.

The PM was speaking while inaugurating an initiative on supporting the NREGS through State Legal Services Authorities. "The NREGS is a historic initiative of our Government. Such a social security programme exists nowhere else in the world," he said.

In his address, Chief Justice of India K G Balakrishnan said the NREGS was one of the finest social security measures for the poor. "We have tried to fight poverty by various means, but have met with little success. So what India needs is something more lasting than patchwork policies to help its millions of poverty-stricken people. The NREGS is one of the means which can solve the problem, given that it has the potential to provide livelihood to millions," he said.

Heading: Terror biggest threat to India’s integrity, fight unitedly: Sonia - Indian Express
Content:
TV news broadcasters took the first major step on Thursday to bring in more accountability through a regulatory system in the electronic media. This would also ensure 'full and fair presentation of news'. A nine member News Broadcasting Standards (Disputes Redressal) Authority, headed by former Chief Justice J S Varma, started operating from Thursday. It would accept complaints against members of TV news channels and take suo motu cognisance of any violations of the 'principles of self-regulation'.

"Self regulation in media is necessary, as it has now become a very powerful source of information and misinformation, so I congratulate NBA for taking this step", said the former Chief Justice. He further pointed out that though anybody whose sensibility is offended by certain news representations can complain to the authority, the latter's jurisdiction and intervention would not be limited to complaints.

Any viewer can send a complaint to the broadcaster within seven days of the telecast of a programme and the broadcaster will be required to reply within a week's time. If the complainant is not satisfied with the response, he can file a complaint before the authority within a fortnight at Rs 1,000 per complaint. The authority, in turn, will be empowered to admonish, warn, censure, express disapproval and/or impose a fine of up to Rs 1 lakh on the broadcaster and/or recommend to the concerned authority for suspension/revocation of license of such a broadcaster.

The NBA's content guidelines call for impartiality and objectivity in reporting, ensuring neutrality in crime reporting in a way that does not induce, glorify, incite or positively depict violence and its perpetrators or have a misleading or desensitising effect, shunning sex and nudity and respecting privacy of individuals. Besides refraining from advocating or encouraging superstition and occultism, anything endangering national security should not be encouraged, says the NBA code. Sting operations have been termed as the 'last resort' and must be in an 'identifiable public interest', the code reads.

The move came after a series of deliberations between the 14 broadcasters, representing 30 channels, under the aegis of the News Broadcasters Association (NBA) on the issue.

Heading: Indo-Nepal panel to expedite Pancheshwar project - Indian Express
Content:
Describing terrorism as the biggest threat to India's integrity, UPA chairperson Sonia Gandhi on Thursday said people should be united in fighting anti-national forces that make use of such incidents to gain political mileage.

Sonia was speaking at the Samajik Kranti Samaroh rally organised by the Haryana Government to launch its flagship programme, Mahatma Gandhi Gramin Basti Yojana, under which 100 square yards plots would be distributed free to SCs, BCs and the poor. "Some people are creating an atmosphere of violence in the country, but no policy based on hatred can succeed. Today, on Gandhi Jayanti, we have to take a pledge not to bow down before such forces," she said.

She commended CM Bhupinder Singh Hooda for launching a number of welfare schemes. Hooda said, October 2, was an auspicious day as Eid coincides with the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi and the launch of the scheme came at an apt time.

Heading: Another Orissa district in grip of violence - Indian Express
Content:
The meeting of the Indo-Nepal Joint Committee on Water Resources in Kathmandu agreed to set up an authority to undertake the 6,000-MW Pancheshwar multi- purpose project on the Mahakali river and expedite work on preparation of the Detailed Project Report (DPR) on Saptkosi High Dam on the Kosi.

"Both sides agreed to set up a joint Pancheshwar Development Authority to undertake the work on the Pancheshwar project on Mahakali river near Uttarakhand-Nepal border," informed Water Resources Secretary Umesh N Panjiar, who led the Indian delegation to Kathmandu. The proposed authority, is likely to be headed by either the Minister of State or the Secretary of the Ministry of Water Resources. The decision on the members of the Indian side will be taken soon.

The Joint River Commission is likely to take a decision on the funding pattern of the project soon. The cost of implementing the Pancheshwar project, estimated at about Rs 17,000 crore in 2002, has now escalated to Rs 30,000 crore.

Both sides reiterated their commitment to expediting the work on preparation of the DPR of Saptkosi High Dam project during the meeting which concluded on Wednesday in Kathmandu. Nepal assured full administrative support and security to Indian engineers.

Heading: Ministry moves to revise creamy layer income criterion - Indian Express
Content:
The fire of communal and ethnic violence continued unabated in Orissa fire as it spread to Boudh district, where about 20 houses belonging to Dalits were burnt down by tribals on Wednesday night.

While Kandhamal remained relatively peaceful on Wednesday and Thursday, the scene of violence shifted to neighbouring Boudh district where the tribals burnt scores of houses in Matakapa village of Kantamala block. Kantamala is close to the Gochhapada police station, which was burnt down by a mob last month.

Director General of Police Manmohan Praharaj, who has been camping in Kandhamal since Wednesday, said the violence in Boudh was not a communal one.

"As far as I know, it was over ethnic issues. We are rushing force to the area," he told The Indian Express. Indefinite curfew has been imposed in Boudh.

The official death toll in the district rose to 32 on Wednesday.

Lalgi Nayak — a Christian, who was attacked by tribals at Rudangia village in Tikabali block of the district — succumbed to the wound on his neck at a hospital in Berhampur on Wednesday night.

In the past two days, 100 people including several members of the Sangh Parivar have been arrested by the police in the district.

"Containing violence is the first priority for me," the DGP said, adding that persons, irrespective of their religion, would be booked if found involved in violence or instigating others. An order has been issued to all licensed gun holders asking them to surrender their weapons at police stations."

Meanwhile, 10 more companies of paramilitary forces are on their way to Kandhamal to step up law and order and security.

On Wednesday, a division bench of the Orissa High Court urged the Centre to send additional forces to ensure peace and calm in Kandhamal.

Kandhamal Superintendent of Police Praveen Kumar said nine areas in the district — including Phulbani town — would continue to be under curfew indefinitely.

"Today curfew was relaxed during the day in all nine police station areas as no untoward incident took place. Night curfew will, however, remain in force," he said.

Heading: Orissa, Karnataka get Lalu, Oscar warning - Indian Express
Content:
The annual income limit for determining the creamy layer among the Other Backward Castes (OBCs) is set to go up from the present Rs 2.5 lakh to Rs 4.5 lakh. A proposal in this regard from the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is scheduled to come before the Cabinet on Friday. The raise in the income ceiling for the creamy layer has been according to the recommendations of the National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC).

The Indian Express was the first to report that the NCBC has recommended the revision of the annual income ceiling for creamy layer among the OBCs from Rs 2.5 lakh to Rs 4.5 lakh. The NCBC had submitted its recommendations to the Centre on July 1 this year.

The revised income ceiling will mean that benefits of reservations in Central educational institutions and jobs in Central Government will be availed by a much larger section of the OBCs. The Centre is in a hurry to implement the revised ceiling in view of the recent Supreme Court directive and also with an eye on the polls. Once it is approved by the Cabinet, it will be communicated to the HRD and DOPT Ministry for issuing appropriate orders to Central educational institutions and regarding employment in Central Government.

This will be the second revision of the income criteria for the creamy layer. The first was undertaken in 2004 that raised the upper limit from Rs 1 lakh to Rs 2.5 lakh. Then, however, the benefits of reservation were limited to jobs. Efforts for a second revision of the income limit came after the HRD Ministry enacted the Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006, in January, 2007, to provide 27 per cent reservation for OBCs in Central educational institutions. The Supreme Court stayed the decision and in its final judgment upheld the Act subject to exclusion of better offs or "creamy layer" among OBCs. Thereafter, the NCBC was asked to review the existing income ceiling to determine the creamy layer and submit its report.

Heading: Christians in MP take to Gandhigiri - Indian Express
Content:
Union Railway Minister Lalu Prasad Yadav and Labour Minister Oscar Fernandes on Thursday warned Orissa and Karnataka governments that the Centre would not hesitate to take stern action and even go beyond Article 355 if attacks on Christians continued in these states.

Addressing a protest march by Christians at Jantar Mantar, Yadav and Fernandes said that they would take up the issue with the Prime Minister during the Cabinet meeting on Friday and urge for immediate measures to stop attacks against the minority community.

"The states have been warned under Article 355. But if they fail to check the violence against Christians then the Centre can go beyond Article 355," Yadav said, indicating use of controversial Article 356 to dismiss a state government and impose President's rule, if the attacks did not stop.

The RJD chief said that during the Cabinet meeting on Friday he would urge the Prime Minister to visit the affected areas or send a delegation. Fernandes assured the community that secular forces were supporting them and that stern action would be taken against the perpetrators.

Lashing out at the Bajranj Dal, Yadav said,"They are a bunch of cowards. Ban them and put them in jail."

The other high point was the presence of CPI(M) politburo member Sitaram Yechury. It was for the first time after the rift over the Indo-US Nuclear deal that Yechury shared the dais with RJD and Congress leaders. Yechury accused the Centre of failing to act and said that the Centre should act if the state Government is "unwilling" or "unable" to check the violence .

Meanwhile, CPI(M) general secretary Prakash Karat on Friday criticised the UPA Government for not doing enough to check the continuing anti-Christian violence in Orissa and Karnataka.

Heading: Woman throws daughters from 6th floor, jumps to death - Indian Express
Content:
Christians in Madhya Pradesh took to Gandhigiri — donating blood, organising human chains and planting saplings — on the Mahatma's birth anniversary on Thursday to protest the violence targeting the community.

Following a prayer meeting in front of a Gandhi statue they donated blood in Bhopal. Similar programmes were held across the state.

The Madhya Pradesh Isai Mahasangh (MPIM), which is spearheading the protests along with many socio-political organisations had earlier decided to send one lakh postcards to politicians and bureaucrats across India, including PM Manmohan Singh, leader of Opposition L K Advani and AICC chairperson Sonia Gandhi, with the message: "Thank you for the riots" printed on it.

However, on Wednesday an MPIM spokesperson said the campaign would reflect the Gandhian way of life with a new message: "Save Christians, may god bless you."

A delegation called on CM Shivraj Singh Chouhan and objected to the recent remarks made by senior BJP leader Thaverchand Gehlot.

Gehlot while addressing the 'Mahakumbha' of BJP workers in Bhopal, had called Christians "anti-nationals" in the presence of Chouhan.

The CM reportedly said he would react only after hearing the recording of Gehlot's speech.

"We will continue to protest till we succeed in creating awareness about atrocities against the Christians by a few anti-social elements in the name of religion," the Mahasangh said.

Mahasangh secretary Pradeep Luther said the community, along with several social and political organisations, will continue with its 'Gandhigiri'.

Spokesperson for Catholic Bishops Council Anand Muttungal alleged that "on the one hand the BJP Government was talking of providing protection to Christians but on the other party leaders were accusing converts of supporting anti-national elements".

The "anti-national" charge was leveled in front of more than two lakh BJP workers causing an immense damage to the community that has worked very hard to educate and empower the Dalits, tribals and other weaker sections of the society, Christian leader A B Tigga said.

The community also demanded immediate arrests of people who torched a cathedral in Jabalpur, and demanded CBI inquiry into attacks on churches in Ratlam and Indore. They alleged that the real culprits were being shielded.

Heading: Ready to accept court verdict, says Rizwanur’s uncle - Indian Express
Content:
A 30-year-old woman threw her daughters from the sixth floor of a building before she herself jumped to death. All three died on the spot, said the police.

In her suicide note, Sunita Arvind Khandagale said she was taking the extreme step because her husband had been unfaithful.

She was living with her husband, in-laws, brother in-law and two daughters — Harshada (5) and Sakshi (4) — in Pudamjee Paradise, Bhavani Peth.

"Sunita said in the suicide note that her husband was having an extra-marital affair with a woman named Sheetal who sent him SMSes and called him up frequently. She also said her body should be handed over to her brother," said Assistant Commissioner of Police Suresh Pote.

"We suspect that she killed her children thinking no one would take care of them after her death. An offence will be registered against her husband Arvind under Section 306 (abetting suicide) of the IPC," Pote added.

On Thursday morning, Arvind left home for work after which Sunita took her daughters to the terrace of the building. She first threw Sakshi, then Harshada, after which she herself jumped from the terrace.

Residents of the building saw them lying in a pool of blood and informed the police and family members.

"The victims died on the spot. Their bodies have been sent for post-mortem," a policeman said.

Heading: Malegaon: Officers revisit areas of ’06 blast arrests - Indian Express
Content:
A day after the CBI appended a "suicide note" by Rizwanur Rehman to the chargesheets against the seven accused naming, among others, his uncle Saidur Rehman as being responsible for his death, Saidur said on Thursday he would accept the court verdict if found guilty.

"There have been allegations against me in the past that I accepted a sum of Rs 21,000 from Ashok Todi for passing on information about Rizwanur and Priyanka Todi. I have been questioned by the CBI, and if they did not chargesheet me I suppose it was because they could not find any wrongdoing on my part. I am a TMC worker and I run an NGO," Saidur said.

The suicide note, retrieved by the CBI from Rizwanur's computer's hard drive from a deleted folder, is said to have been written on September 20, 2007 — a day before his body was found. The note names Saidur, then DC (HQ) Gyanwant Singh, then DC (DD) Ajay Kumar, then assistant commissioner Sukanti Chakraborty (since retired), SI Krishnendu Das, Todi associate Anil Saraogi and TMC MLA Javed Ahmed Khan as being "morally responsible" for his death.

Heading: Soft on error - Indian Express
Content:
Yet to achieve a breakthrough in investigations into Monday night's blast in Malegaon, agencies are now looking for leads in areas from which the nine men arrested for their alleged involvement in the September 8, 2006, blasts in the textile town were picked up.

They have launched combing operations in these areas and are also questioning dealers of LML Freedom — the make of the two-wheeler on which the explosive device was planted — in Ahmednagar and Shreerampur districts, sources revealed.

According to police sources, Jafar Nagar, Golden Nagar and Naya Bazaar are some of the areas currently being combed for leads. These areas are occupied by a large number of Muslim families who originally hail from Azamgarh in Uttar Pradesh and are employed in the powerloom sector.

According to police, Riyaz Arsalan, Ishtiaq Ahmed Mohammed and SIMI's former Malegaon president Munavar Ahmed — the three absconding youths named in the chargesheet filed by the state Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS) in the 2006 blasts — lived in these areas.

The police have also established that the production of LML Freedom had stopped in 2005 and that a limited number of dealers still selling it were in Ahmednagar and Shreerampur.

The Road Transport Offices of these districts provided the ATS details of these dealers. Besides conducting enquiries with the dealers, a buyer was also questioned by the police, sources said.

Meanwhile, a 22-year old waiter from Nayapura was questioned and his statement recorded today as part of a magesterial probe being conducted.

The youth, identified as Iqbal, works at Nisar Dairy, and had allegedly been asked by the owner of a Shakeel Transport to inform the local police chowki about an unclaimed bike parked in the area. Iqbal's statement that he had gone to the chowki and informed the police is being verified.

Heading: Ash Thursday - Indian Express
Content:
There's leadership in the Congress and the government it runs, isn't there? In that case now is the time the party and government leadership must step in and stamp on a dangerous political misadventure some Congress leaders appear to have embarked on. It is no one's case that in a democracy police/security agency actions can't be questioned. But how are a bunch of disgruntled Congressmen, including two Union Ministers and a general secretary, murmuring, whispering and talking of questions about the Jamia Nagar police operation going about it? They are the ruling party, nationally and in Delhi, the Union home minister was in police HQ when the operation was conducted, the police in Delhi and several other states are conducting investigations, the courts will hear the case and those charged with terror acts will have full and, by all accounts, high-quality legal representation — given all this and given the absence of one shred of credible evidence that questions the operation, how on earth can senior Congress leaders all but trash it? The encounter happened under the watch of the Congress-led government and if Ministers disagree with it, they should quit and tell us what we don't know. Their prattle is immensely irresponsible and if re-election worries of some Congressmen are at the source of this, the irresponsibility gets bigger.

The worst effect of this twisted political correctness is that it has the potential to destroy the space and the possibility of recognising the complexity of the problem. The young men of Indian Mujahideen carried all the markers of aspirational Indians. If we had many, many more young Muslims with their kind of CVs, we would not need Sachar committees. But these men were still ultra-radicalised — why? This is a question politics needs to ask and find answers to. Not a politics of tokenism which is grievously unfair to the Muslim community; it makes it appear that the community is comfortable with the radicalised fringe, when that's plainly not the case. Indian Muslim identity is a marvellous mosaic and it cannot be allowed to be subsumed by questions about terrorism. The politically cynical/politically correct lot pose as much threat to this as the Hindu fundamentalist.

So the Congress leadership has to signal that someone is in charge, that police and security forces have political backing in a difficult fight, that the multi-state investigative effort that's on is a positive development. And that the country comes before any constituency.

Heading: Stock replies - Indian Express
Content:
The lights are going out all over India, and we will not see them lit again in our — possibly lengthened — lifetimes. The most demonised of minorities, already crushed under the weight of punitive taxation and social opprobrium, is now further marginalised; India's crusading health minister has dragooned us into joining the 70-plus countries with nationwide restrictions on smoking in "public" places.

When US states, beginning with California in 1999, started banning indoor smoking, I began keeping a small if slightly obsessive spreadsheet of the places in the world where I would like to live but couldn't till I gave up smoking. Ireland, the home of pubs filled with what Seamus Heaney called "gregarious smoke", became the first entire country to ban indoor smoking in 2004; and as the usual progressive suspects — Norway, New Zealand and the like — started implementing similar restrictions, I began to feel quite unwanted.

It was difficult to avoid the feeling that an era was ending. Ever since Walter Raleigh popularised it in the Elizabethan court — earning for his effort the privilege of being cursed in song by a John Lennon in suffering from cigarette-induced insomnia ("such a stupid git") — tobacco, like alcohol, has become intertwined with society, with tradition and social ritual. In the dandyish, degenerate Regency period, men duelled over the aesthetics of snuffboxes. The trenches of World War I may have developed superstitions about how many cigarettes you could light with one match. Tobacco has symbolised, at different times and places, friendship, peace, sexual availability, and capitalist greed. Physicians prescribed it for asthma, for ulcers, for all manner of nervous disorders. All popular depictions of FDR featured a shawl across his withered knees, and a cigarette holder held at a jaunty angle in his mouth; a New York Times profile of Kamaraj in the '60s featured his addiction to Gold Flakes. Queen Victoria detested it, and banned it from royal palaces; Adolf Hitler, a man of slightly larger ambitions, launched massive anti-smoking campaigns, complete with all the bells and whistles his propaganda machine could provide. (Thus, if you are forced, at some point, to call someone turning up their nose at your cigarette a Nazi, it is at least less unfair than when the word is generally thrown about.) And, of course, Gandhiji famously stole money for cigarettes when a teenager.

In a way it is extraordinary that something which has had such awesome cultural impact over centuries should have retreated so swiftly. It had been known since 1828 that nicotine was poisonous; and yet, even after the US surgeon-general released the first official condemnation in 1964, it took a while for anything to happen — till the flurry of bans and prohibitions over the past decade, the blink of an eye in historical time. That might explain the puzzling persistence of enclaves where smoking around others is still considered acceptable. The more conservative — or the more libertarian — areas of America, for example: a map of that country in which counties that have banned smoking are in blue and others are in red will look frighteningly familiar to anyone who's followed the past couple of presidential elections. It also explains the stunned, vaguely outraged expression on the faces that you will see puffing away on Indian roads. Like an investment-banker demanding a bailout, they never thought the crash would come, at least not in their lifetime.

Unquestionably, something about smoking has turned otherwise liberal people into whole-hearted believers in heavy-handed government intervention. One would think that government-imposed bans rarely work. Yes, in Scotland, as Dr Ramadoss cheerfully informed us, 45,000 people tried to stop in the months following its smoking ban. Unfortunately, Dr Ramadoss failed to complete the statistic: only 18 per cent of those did so successfully. Well, Dr Ramadoss would say, in the end the ban is to protect non-smokers as well, particularly those whose workplaces are unhealthy cesspools of viciously selfish smokers. Difficult to argue with that; though the definition of "public place" and "workplace" seems so arbitrary. Tellingly, there is no attempt to deal with the fact that in a country where domestic service is still quite common, one person's home is frequently someone else's workplace — but servants are invisible in India, so that's OK.

And government actions always have unintended consequences: in Ireland, it is estimated that over a thousand pubs shut down following the 2004 nationwide ban. The vast majority were in small, isolated hamlets, and, in doing so, they deprived those already-fracturing communities of a vital form of social glue. In New York, midtown pavements began to be unusable for pedestrians when they had to navigate around the entire smoking population of giant skyscrapers. India, in any case, has barely begun to develop a sense of "public place": a country with the extremes of social and economic inequality that ours possesses has trouble providing places that can be considered both "public" and "secure". Consider the madness that will result in which genuinely public spaces — pavements, the open road — will

replace supposedly public spaces — malls, say — as a place where smokers will congregate. It is unlikely that the number of places that can genuinely be considered shared will expand. Here, as ever, Central government diktat is no replacement for local or commercial decision-making — or even for basic courtesy.

An earlier spate of tobacco-related bans — on advertising — is sadly illustrative: cricket lost Benson and Hedges, tennis Virginia Slims, Nascar RJR and Formula One pretty much everything. Smaller sports were disproportionately affected: international snooker was so badly hit it demanded special treatment. Tobacco's been so intertwined with modern life that trying to remove it surgically, without some costs, was never an option.

My spreadsheet of places that don't live and let light is too long to be informative, now. When New York banned smoking in 2003, I told myself that I needn't worry, I'd give up when Boston did so. Massachusetts banned smoking in 2005; I told myself I'd wait for Delhi — like that would ever happen. After years of smoking in the freezing rain and scalding heat, of choosing friends and favourite places because of tobacco, of restlessness in long movies and interminable night walks looking for open paanwallas, I think Dr Ramadoss has just taken away my last excuse. Thanks, doctor. Thanks a lot.

mihir.sharma@expressindia.com

Heading: Policing for peanuts - Indian Express
Content:
The CPM has long suffered from a gap between rhetoric and action wide enough to attract the most determined arbitrageur. When the CPM general secretary, Prakash Karat, wrote about the perceived dangers of the new pension scheme and warned the aam admi about the stock market, he presumably meant that the party — the vanguard, after all, of proletarian revolution — was above such concerns. Alas, if only it were so! But perhaps, it's good for the CPM that it isn't. We are more than willing to grant that the end of history hasn't come. We are also willing to grant that the spectres of Marx will be around, perhaps for the better. The CPM itself long gave up the goal of the proletarian state and accepted its role and destiny as a party within a democracy, run by a market economy. But it seems that while most of the comrades have come a good distance, some comrades haven't even begun the long march yet.

But if that assumption is untrue, the picture becomes grim indeed. Are Prakash Karat and M.K. Pandhe then guilty of doublespeak? The doublespeak that tells the aam admi: "It's all right if we do it, but it's not your cup of tea." Maybe, but the more optimistic amongst us will see it as a redemptive pragmatism. There is then no other means of explaining why the party would warn us to lay off but enjoy the incremental returns of speculating in the stock market through the proxy of mutual funds. The CPM's defence that it invests only in public sector funds can't hold water as those same funds prefer private sector entities in their portfolios.

The CPM's rhetoric does not do justice to the CPM itself. The party deserves to be bracketed with others of the economic mainstream. But its leaders just don't seem to have the will to say as much.

Heading: Moonlight melody - Indian Express
Content:
Words have a way of coming into fashion unannounced. In September 2006, Prime Minister Manmohan Singh remarked, "Unless the 'beat constable' is brought into the vortex of our counter-terrorist strategy, our capacity to pre-empt future attacks would be severely limited." This was quickly picked up by the media, and the "beat constable" was placed in the centre of the public debate on national security.

There is, however, a disconnect between what the prime minister says, and what the government does. The police constable currently earns between Rs 3050-4590, at par with lowest categories of government employees. The Sixth Pay Commission, in its great munificence, has recommended a hike of about Rs 150-310 in the constable's scales, increasing his pay to between Rs 3200-4900. This is the bright side. Many states have scales well below centrally stipulated levels. Gujarat, for instance, has a current scale of Rs 2750-4400. There are rare exceptions, like in Kerala, where the scale stands at Rs 5930-9590.

Not only are constables grossly underpaid; they suffer abysmal working conditions. Across India, "housing satisfaction" for the police — the proportion of serving personnel who are provided family quarters — stands at a disgraceful 29.3 per cent. In India's capital — boasting "global city" ambitions — it is an even lower 19.97 per cent. Thus, a majority of constables leave their families behind in their villages, seeing them rarely, on grudgingly provided leaves of absence. Those who bring their families to their place of posting, particularly in cities, end up living in illegal slums and tenements. Thus, the very condition of their daily existence constitutes a breach of the law!

Working conditions are no better. Outside the metropolis, facilities in police stations are, at best, rudimentary. In rural areas — particularly in ill-governed states — the police operate out of structures that are often worse than cattle sheds. Here, a BPR&D study notes, "across the country... they are asked to put in consistently 16 to 18 hours of duty on a continuous basis". In many police stations and posts, far from fighting the terrorists and insurgents they are routinely pitted against, policemen lack even the minimal capacities to defend themselves. Since a majority of constables retire at the rank at which they join, only a small proportion attains the rank of head constable; a miniscule number rises to the rank of sub-inspector or inspector. Career frustration adds to this deadly cocktail.

There is, moreover, a complete mismatch between the criteria of recruitment and training on the one hand, and the increasing complexity of the tasks a modern police force is required to handle. The minimum qualification for recruitment is a Class 10 pass; some states have pushed that up to 12; a few have reduced it to 8 so that "rural people have better chances of getting the job". These barely literate recruits are variously pushed through around a year of "training" (this has, in at least one case, been reduced to six months) that principally consists of marching up and down on a parade ground, physical training, arms training (in many cases, comprising just a single field firing practice) and a few desultory lectures on police regulations and law.

The constable, moreover, has been transformed, through sustained processes of class denigration by the media, the courts, the political leadership and what passes for "civil society", into an object of widespread contempt and, as one serving police officer expresses it, into a "convenient lightning rod that attracts the charged fury of our so-called civil society". In sum, the constable operates in "the most degrading conditions that can be humanly inflicted, in one of the most volatile societies in the world".

And this constable — barely educated, ill-trained, ill-equipped and held in wide contempt — is expected to effectively tackle a 21st century scourge like terrorism. Indeed, he is expected to do this while displaying a sophisticated understanding of the niceties of the law, and the subtle exercise of powers relating to arrest, custody, search, seizure, bail, surveillance and the use of force!

In our age of liberalisation and globalisation, this makes sense: you get what you pay for. India is not paying for a modern and efficient policing system. India is not paying for a professional policeman. India is not paying for security. India cannot, consequently, be secure. The beat constable in India will have to be reinvented, in terms of educational and training profiles, equipment, living and working conditions and, crucially, his status in society, before he can be "brought into the vortex of our counter-terrorist strategy".  

The writer is executive director, Institute for Conflict Management & the South Asia Terrorism Portal
