His outburst against both Sonia Gandhi and Hooda had come as a shock to the Congress high command. But Hooda had managed to quell the rebellion and get Arvind Sharma to vote in favour of the UPA.

Heading: Binding threads - Indian Express
Content:
The Haryana Chief Minister Bhupinder Singh Hooda today said that he would soon talk to the representatives of the Tata Company to persuade them to set up the Nano car project in the state. "Every facility would be provided to the company," he said.

Hooda, who was talking to the mediapersons after a foundation stone laying ceremony in Sirsa today, said that the Paddy procurement had commenced in the state and all arrangements had been made to provide every facility to the farmers and traders in all the mandis.

He directed the officers to ensure that there should not be any problem regarding lifting of paddy and shortage of bags, etc. The Central Government would soon announce bonus on paddy and it would be more than that of last year, he hoped.

In reply to a question regarding Lok Sabhaelections, Hooda said All the 10 Lok Sabha seats in the State would be won by the Congress party.

Heading: Makkar to approach PM , Prez again - Indian Express
Content:
Designer wear from across the border is hot and Pakistan is the next shopping destination.Shaheen P Parshadchecks out the trend

Boundaries may have divided the population of India and Pakistan, but the common culture that binds the diverse sub-continent together continues to act like an invisible glue. And for those of us who forget this fact, a Pakistani woman sporting a Banarsi sari or an Indian woman emitting sheer grace in a Pakistani salwar kameez is a ready reminder. Take for instance Aroosa Alam and Peenaz Masani flaunting the best of Indian art and Shabana Azmi flaunting her beautiful Pakistani drapes. The trend is getting more pronounced, with traditional clothing from across the fence flooding Indian markets and vice-versa.

India's Ritu Kumar and Pakistan's Nadia Lakdawala are some of the most sought after designers being approached with lucrative orders by customers from the other side of the border. The rich and the fashion-conscious form a majority of their clientele, who mainly look for what is unique to the other country. As a result, there is a growing demand for Indian Silk saris and ghagra cholis in Pakistan, while in India, it is the zardosi and meenakari-studded dresses and Peshawari juttis that are much in demand. The prices match the status of the clients, with prices ranging between Rs 4,000 and Rs 25,000 (INR).

Gita Sud, an Amritsar-based designer, who has been dressing up Pakistanis for quite sometime now, attributes this trend to a thirst for "the different". Apart from Amritsari cut-work and embroidery, a large number of people from Pakistan also came to India to shop for Banarasi saris, she says. "The craze is more among the Pakistani youth, especially girls, who are known to go ga-ga over Indian pashmina silk saris and come with their parents to India to shop for their weddings," she says.

The craze is mutual, she adds, "I have friends and customers, who often go to Pakistan to shop for clothes for special occasions. I have a client, Roshni, who has been to Pakistan innumerable times for shopping. "All of the special occasions in their family are famous for showcasing Indian and Pakistani designer clothes side by side," she says.

Anjali Kapoor, a boutique owner, says clothes done in vegetable dyes too are a big hit with the Pakistani public. "In fact, each state has its own specialty, which has of late been attracting many Pakistani customers," she explains. She says that as far as Indians' craze for Pakistani threads is concerned, their bridal wear is more in demand in India these days. The intricate thread, gold and glasswork, which is done by village women in Pakistan, is also very popular here as these are rare in India, she adds.

Hina Anjum, a designer from Pakistan, who recently held an exhibition in Amritsar, says Pakistani designers see better prospects in India, because of which many of them are coming here to hold exhibitions and look for customers. During her four tours to India she has gathered a large number of clients, particularly politicians. "Durability is another factor that comes into the equation here," she says. "Nadia Lakdawala is a known name in India now as she has held several exhibitions in India and also proposes to enter the Indian market in a more direct manner," she says.

Hina says the craze can well be judged from the fact that the orders that she received during her recent exhibition in Delhi far outnumbered what she had received barely a couple of months ago. "I have been flooded with orders of designer suits, particularly items that can be given away as gifts," she says.

"We have also hosted several Indian designers who have a great following in Pakistan," she says. Designers like Tarun Tahiliani, Rohit Bal, Manish Malhotra and Suneet Varma have their designer wear stocked at various renowned outlets in Pakistan. "Ritu Kumar's bridal creations are a rage in Karachi and surrounding areas," she adds.

As for the men, Gunbir Singh, vice-chairman, CII, Punjab, says, "While there is something common in the dress and culture on both sides of the border, it's the intricacies in art work that set the two apart," he says. "Pakistani stuff is rough and tough, quite liked for kurta pyjamas here," he said. Om Prakash Lati Shah, a trader, who often commutes between India and Pakistan, says a lot of men in India have a penchant for Pakistani salwar kameez.

Amritsari shawls add warmth to Indo-Pak relations

Pashminas, jamawars and embroidered shawls manufactured in Amritsar are finding their way into the Pakistani market in large numbers. Though seasonal by nature, the shawl industry of Amritsar depends mainly on orders from Pakistan and other international orders from USA, Middle East, Japan, Australia and Europe.

The once-thriving industry may have been hit hard by the unwarranted policies of the government here, but has found solace in Pakistan, one of the biggest markets for its wares.

Yogesh Mehra, a shawl manufacturer, says that initially Kashmiri shawls dominated the market, but persistence and hard work of the manufacturers here, coupled with innovations in the business, have been able to make a place for the shawls from the holy city in the Pakistani market.

Vijay Saini, another shawl manufacturer, says, "Our hand embroidered shawls are as much in demand in Pakistan owing to constant innovation in design and form." Even the machine-made ones sell like hot cakes. "Stoles, which are smaller in size as compared to shawls and may or may not be woollen, have become a huge hit among global customers and are the latest rage in the fashion circuit in India as well as Pakistan," he claims.

Heading: Another airport proposed for Punjab - Indian Express
Content:
Sikhs in Haryana propose to set up a makeshift office in Kurukshetra on Oct 8

The controversy relating to a separate Haryana Sikh Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (HSGPC) may erupt into a major issue in the coming days, with Shiromani Gurdwara

Parbandhak Committee today stating that it is keeping a close watch on the proposed setting up of makeshift office of HSGPC at Kurukshetra on October 8.

The SGPC is also in a mood to take up the issue with the Centre afresh.

"We are seeking the intervention of Prime Minister Dr Manmohan Singh and that of President Pratibha Patil on the issue," said SGPC chief Avtar Singh Makkar, adding that they were keeping a close eye on the developments taking place in the neighbouring state. "We know that it is the Congress that is behind the whole conspiracy to break the SGPC into two, but it must be understood that the consequences of such a move would have far-reaching effects," warned Makkar.

He said the SGPC would not sit silent if any office for the HSGPC was set up. On the other hand, SGPC member from Kurukshetra, Didar Singh Nalwi, spearheading the movement for the separate body in Haryana, said they were holding their meeting late in the evening today to chalk out their next course of action.

The SGPC also foresees that a separate HSGPC in Haryana will shrink its influence and control over gurdwaras in the region.

Its revenue, collected from "golaks" (donation boxes) put up at shrines, would also come down, affecting the religious body financially.

On the other hand, Haryana's Sikhs wants the money collected from golaks in gurdwaras in state to be spent on Haryana's gurdwaras only. Makkar, however, set the record straight and said the SGPC was spending more money on development, education, evangelism than it was drawing from golaks.

Experts, meanwhile, feel that apart from financial losses, the SGPC's claim of being the only paramount body of the Sikhs will get a major beating with the formation of a separate Sikh body.

Incidentally, the SGPC is also seeking permission from the Centre to allow it to maintain Sikh shrines in Bangladesh, Afghanistan and Pakistan.

Heading: Badal leaves Bains to clear the air on ‘CM-FM’ issue - Indian Express
Content:
The state will soon have another airport between Payal and Sahnewal. Initially planned to be a domestic airport, the airport will later be developed into an international one. Besides, a township, "aeropolis", is planned to be developed near this airport.

Sources said the Union Ministry of Civil Aviation and the Prime Minister's Office has cleared this proposal and it is awaiting a nod from the Ministry of Defence, which is likely to be given soon. Also, this is for the first time that a new township will also come along with the proposed airport. To start with, the airport would be spread over 5,000 acres, but the total size would be around 12,000 acres spread in Ludhiana and Fatehgarh districts.

The proposed airport will be just at 70 km air distance from the Mohali international airport, whereas as per the norms of civil aviation, the minimum distance should be 250 km.

Sources said some time back a company, Bengal Aeropolis, had made a presentation to Punjab Chief Minister Parkash Singh Badal, after which an MoU was signed between them and PSIDC. This company is making a similar township with airport at Durgapur in West Bengal.

Heading: NRI couple held with 3.7 kg heroin from Toronto-bound flight - Indian Express
Content:
Chief Minister Parkash Singh Badal today called upon all politicians to be like IAS officers, who, he said, "may belong to different groups but when one is in trouble, they lend a helping hand. This is what we politicians should learn to do".

In town to inaugurate a daily Punjabi newspaper, the CM seemed to be in a sermonising mood and urged the media to play its role in society.

Congress president Mohinder Singh Kaypee and a battery of Akali leaders, including Minister for Information and Broadcasting Bikram Singh Majithia, SGPC chief Avtar Singh Makkar and Minister for Jails Hira Singh Gabria, were present on the occasion.

While Badal hurriedly left the venue, he left behind media advisor Harcharan Bains to clear the air over the CM versus FM issue. And, Bains took great pains to explain, "There are no differences between the Finance Minister and the Chief Minister. The CM has never snubbed the FM. Rather, I would say that the CM has never snubbed any of his ministers."

Replying to a volley of questions relating to Badal's statement on subsidies, Bains said, "The CM did not snub the FM over this issue. He just spoke about the party's stand on subsidies and that is all."

Chief Minister Parkash Singh Badal laying the foundation stone of a modern bus stand in Hoshiarpur on Sunday. On the occasion, Badal unveiled a massive plan of Rs 5,500 crore to provide water supply, sewerage, streetlights and storm water drainage in the state. Addressing the gathering, Badal said the SAD-BJP government was committed to provide excellent infrastructure in the state. Transport Minister Master Mohan Lal said the ultra-modern air-conditioned bus stand would be constructed at a cost of Rs 7 crore and Punjab Roadways would bear the entire expenditure for this project. He said the construction work of Rajpura, Bathinda, Rampura Phul and Anandpur Sahib bus stands is under execution. He added that the state government would launch air-conditioned bus service from November 1 at a nominal fare.

Heading: All eyes set on the LS polls - Indian Express
Content:
An NRI couple, Raminder Singh Nagra (60) and his wife Harjinder Kaur Nagra (56), were today nabbed with 3.7 kg of heroin from Air India's Amritsar-Birmingham-Toronto flight at Rajasansi International Airport here.

The flight was about to take off when Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) sleuths arrived and stopped the flight from taking off. The DRI team, headed by Superintendent Ramesh Kumar, asked the couple to deplane with their luggage. The flight took off as per schedule.

The culprits hail from Patti Sarain village under Nakodar police station of Jalandhar district. They said their son had packed their luggage and they were not aware about the narcotics.

The DRI sources said that couple had visited Canada several times in the past and their one son is settled in Toronto. "They were visiting him and the narcotics were concealed in the luggage bags," said the DRI officials. Airport Director Arun Talwar said the doors of the aircraft, a Boeing 777-200, had been closed and it was preparing to take off when the pilot was told by the air traffic control (ATC) to return as directed by the DRI.

A case under the NDPS Act has been registered.

Heading: ‘India’s strategic nuclear programme will not be affected’ - Indian Express
Content:
State Congress General House today drew up strategy for the upcoming Lok Sabha elections and decided to highlight the UPA government's performance and the nuclear deal in the run up to polls.

The General House was held after a gap of three years but some of the senior leaders, including former Chief Minister Virbhadra Singh, remained conspicuous by their absence.

Meanwhile, Union Minister of State for External Affairs Anand Sharma stole the limelight and was extended a warm reception.

Pradesh Congress Committee president Kaul Singh Thakur said during the party doors were open for all those who had left the party during the Assembly elections in December 2007 and those who fell in line with the party ideology. Kaul Singh also stressed on strengthening party membership drive and preparation for the polls and claimed the party was in position to put up a serious fight against the BJP.

Sharma talked about UPA government's contribution for development of the state, where approval for Manali-Leh link, four national highways, IIT and central university were highlighted. Some other absentees from the meeting included former MP Chandresh Kumari, G. S. Bali, G. R. Musafir andformer PCC president Viplove Thakur.

Heading: Under utilisation of local area development funds - Indian Express
Content:
Union Minister of state for External Affairs Anand Sharma today said the Indo-Us nuclear deal will not affect India's strategic nuclear programme. He also reiterated India's stand on unilateral moratorium on nuclear testing.

Addressing a press conference, Sharma said India has reserved its sovereign right to keep its nuclear reactors. India will continue to retain its right for clinical separation of its reactors for civilian and strategic use till 2014, he added.

Terming the signing of the Indo-US nuclear deal as a historic move for India, the minister counselled the opponents of the deal, especially L.K.Advani, to stop misleading the people. "The deal is very transparent and protects India's strategic needs, opening new doors for civilian nuclear trade with global players," he said.

On asking when will President George Bush sign the legislation on the deal, he said, "It's just a matter of procedure and would take maximum a one or two days."

The minister said the way India has positioned itself globally, it has emerged as a winner in its diplomatic efforts. The agreement with France has already been signed and formalities have been completed to sign deal with Russia.

After UK Prime Minister Gordon Brown's meeting with Prime Minister Dr Manmohan Singh, India will sign the deal with UK. "This is a big achievement for India as there are other countries awaiting to sign similar deals," he added.

Sharma did not agree that China is opposed to the NSG approval. "China had refused to grant approval, but China has also supported us,"he said.

Earlier, delivering a lecture on Indo-US nuclear deal, organised by Rajiv Gandhi Study Centre, Sharma said, NSG, headed by US President was established to stop India from developing its civilian nuclear technologies. But now the US Congress has agreed to sign the pact, after taking due safeguards for its strategic nuclear programme."

Heading: Opinion of law dept sought on controversial CD case - Indian Express
Content:
Himachal Pradesh government has earned the Centre's ire for being slow in implementation of the projects approved under the MP Local Area Development(MPLAD) Fund and asked for timely completion of the works to avoid under-utilisation of the funds.

Union Minister of state for External Affairs Anand Sharma, who held a meeting with state government officials to review utilisation of the MPLAD funds (Rajya Sabha), noted that of total 245 works approved and Rs 6.25 crore sanctioned, only 67 works amounting to Rs 1.54 crore were finally completed. The state has received Rs 7 crore from the funds till now. He said to get more funds under the scheme, timely submission of utilisation certificate is a must.

Union Minister said it was a matter of concern that 178 works were pending, 41 works (schemes) could not started due to land dispute, non-availability of land and delay in signing of agreement with the panchayats.

"The government agencies should see the feasibility of the works in a month time and if the work are not started, it should be reported to Deputy Commissioner Office, Shimla, so that the money is not reallocated for other works," he said. Sharma said 137 works were in progress at different stages, some of these have been completed, but the utilisation certificates are still awaited.

He claimed that the funds were not a constraint and adequate money would be given for the upgrading Municipal Corporation Shimla's Laboratory.

He approved Rs 2.50 lakh for purchase of vehicle for Shimla Municipal Corporation for sterilisation of stray dogs and Rs 5 lakh for the completion of ambulance road. He directed the PWD authorities to complete the playground and retaining wall work of Kendriya Vidayalya, Shimla for which Rs 15 lakh has been sanctioned.

Heading: Himachal confidential - Indian Express
Content:
Himachal's BJP government is not going by the report of the state's Vigilance and Anti-Corruption bureau relating to the controversial CD which was released by former minister Major (retd) Vijai Singh Mankotia during last year's Hamirpur Lok Sabha by-election.

To make the case foolproof, state's home department, headed by Chief Minister Prem Kumar Dhumal, has decided to seek the opinion of the law department before taking a final view on registration of an FIR.

The Vigilance and Anti-Corruption bureau had got a voice test done on the CD from a Chandigarh-based central Forensic Laboratory. The bureau sent its report to the government, enclosing the CFSL findings about voice samples of former chief minister Virbhadra Singh in August. Mankotia, who now also faces a defamation case instituted against him by Virbhadra Singh, had levelled charges of corruption against the former chief minister and his family members—-whose voice, he claimed, had been dubbed in the CD. A retired IAS officer deposed before the Vigilance providing vital clues about "authenticity" of the contents in the CD.

In its report sent to the government, the Vigilance Bureau had asked for permission to register an FIR for thorough investigation of the CD.

The Chief Minister, however, asked the home department to get the entire issue examined from legal aspects. "If the law department tells us to tighten up the case by getting more evidence and plugging loopholes, the case may go back to the Vigilance," said an official in the home department.

Heading: ADB to invest $ 90 m for tourism - Indian Express
Content:
The transfer UFO

Bureaucratic circles have been hit by the 'transfer UFO' or transfer due to unfound objective these days that has struck twice recently to cast a shadow on stable postings of the officers. The latest case being Harinder Hira, Principal Secretary Food and Civil Supplies who lost charge of all four departments held by her including Environment and the additional charge of Urban Development, Housing and Town and Country Planning. In previous reshuffle the UFO struck Ram Subhag Singh who had lost charge of MD Tourism.

Helicopter survey is in fashion

When Horticulture Minister Narender Bragta was asked the reason why Chief Minister did not visit the rain affected areas of Shimla district, he said, "I asked him not to go as it was not safe, the roads were treacherous". What about an air survey? "It sounds fashionable but it does not help in getting in touch with people directly. Though many like to be photographed in helicopter on such surveys." At the same time the state government is finding it hard to find a replacement for its present helicopter that has developed snags at many points and no one wants to risk a ride.

Hogging the limelight

As the Congress held first General House in past three years to make the strategy for the future Lok Sabha elections on Sunday, BJP too strategically scheduled its State Executive Meeting on the same day. The BJP leaders did not accept the objective to be "petty" and one leader said, "The BJP is in no way behind its competitor in futuristic political planning."

Bali in full control

Former Transport Minister G.S. Bali's claims that his unexpected appearance at a BJP's public function in his constituency in Kangra district established he was in full control of his constituency. But the analysts in both the parties are studying his behavior, first in context of his proximity to Dhumal and secondly, in context of his absence at various important events of Congress such as swearing in of party president, two months ago.

The political push

Former CM Virbhadra Singh comments on Prem Kumar Dhumal's attempts to promote his son MP Anurag Thakur as the prospective CM has attracted a lot of criticism across political circles. Singh has also been under attack of similar allegations in respect of his wife's political career.

Heading: On the bus between Mumbai and Pune, guard your laptop - Indian Express
Content:
The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has agreed to invest over US $ 90 million for development of tourism infrastructure in Himachal Pradesh. Chief Minister Prem Kumar Dhumal in a statement released today said after his meeting with the five-member ADB team.

The team is lead by Michael Green and includes Mustafa Ahmed, Gurmeet Rai, Vidhwanathan and Bhuminathan. It has visited over 60 sites across eight districts since August.

The ADB's roadmap for tourism in state includes identification of various tourism circuits and allied tourism promotion activities. The CM said, "The bank intended to create and enhance institutional and regulatory frameworks useful for promotion of environmentally and culturally sustainable, socially inclusive and financially viable tourism."

Heading: Woman held for mobile theft - Indian Express
Content:
Laptops of Prasad Ghanorkar and Jaishree Biradar, who had boarded two Mumbai-bound buses to Pune early Friday morning, were stolen during the journey. Upon reaching Mumbai, both filed complaints at the Matunga police station. However, while the police is investigating Ghanorkar's case, Biradar will have to get in touch with the Pune rural police as her case has been transferred there.

The Matunga police receive regular complaints of laptop thefts on Pune-Mumbai buses and rely on the 'statement of the complainant' to decide whether they would investigate the case themselves or to transfer it to the Pune police.

"Both Ghanorkar and Biradar had boarded buses around the same time and it is possible that the theft was committed by the same person. However, while Biradar in her statement has said that she was certain that her laptop was stolen between Pune and Lonavla, Ghanrokar realised that his laptop was stolen only when the bus reached the Dadar depot. Depending on their statements, we have transferred Biradar's case to Pune, while Ghanorkar's case will stay with us for investigation," said police inspector Pramod Koparde from Matunga police station.

According to the Matunga police at least a couple of such thefts are reported every month and this year around 8-10 cases have already been reported.

"We are forced to transfer most of the laptop theft cases to the Pune police as most of them occur during the initial part of the journey, either at the Pune depot, or at Lonavla where the buses stop for refreshments," said senior police inspector SL Deshmukh from Matunga police station. While the FIR is registered here, the case papers are sent to the Pune Rural Superintendent's office and the complainants are expected to keep in touch with the Pune officials.

Owing to the increase in such cases, the Matunga police have also stationed two policemen, one of them in plain clothes, at the bus stand.

According to SL Deshmukh, "They keep a tab on suspicious characters and can be immediately approached if someone discovers that one has been robbed. This is to ensure that such thefts do not occur in Pune-bound buses originating from Mumbai." He went on to add, "So far, we have transferred a large number of cases to Pune, but not many cases are transferred to us by the Pune police."

Biradar, a training manager at a finance and insurance firm has almost reconclied to the fact that she will not get her laptop back, despite knowing the time of the theft and identifying the thief.

"As I boarded the bus I saw a man sitting on the seat adjacent to me suddenly stand up. He was poorly dressed, stank and kept shifting from one seat to another and even tried to help me while I was putting my laptop bag on the baggage shelf. I could see my bag on the top and did not realise when the man had disembarked. It was only at Lonavla, when I opened my bag and saw that my laptop and the charger were missing," recalled Biradar.  

She went on to add, "I was clueless about whom I should complain to and came straight to the Matunga police station. I didn't expect the procedure will be diverted to the Pune police."

Heading: World’s first angioplasty patient visits city - Indian Express
Content:
The railway police caught a woman on Friday and confiscated a mobile from her possession after a complaint was filed by a woman commuter of Borivali- bound local.

According to the arrested woman, she is a TV artist and has many serials up her sleeves. She claims that she is not a thief.

The 27-year-old TV artist is a resident of Ganesh Nagar in Charkop. When the train reached Malad station, one commuter Shraddha Dattaram Parab, resident of Goregaon, who was standing at the footboard found a lady quietly taking out her mobile from her bag. Parab caught her immediately and the mobile fell from the woman's hand. She picked up her mobile, but in the meanwhile the train slowed down at Malad station. Before the train stopped at the station, the woman jumped out from the train. But Shraddha did not leave her. She also jumped out of the train and after a quick chase, caught her, according to the police.

Senior police inspector, Borivali, SR Gaikwad, , said, "One mobile has been found from her possession. The inquiry is going on in this matter, but police have registered a case against the woman under 379 of Indian Penal Code."

Heading: RBI employee gets six months SI in cheque bounce case - Indian Express
Content:
At 38, Bachmann became the world's first patient to undergo angioplasty

Undergoing angioplasty may not be a cause for alarm now-a-days, but it's surprising that a farmer from a Switzerland village was brave enough to face this method which was never tried before then. Doelf Bachmann, who is in town as part of the Eighth International Conference on Coronary Artery Disease, volunteered to undergo the surgery 30 years ago and hasn't looked back since.

According to him, he had lived a rather active and hardworking life. However, by the time he turned 38 in 1977, he started suffering from chest pains and got admitted to the University of Zurich Hospital. The doctors at the hospital told him that he had to undergo a bypass surgery. A night before his surgery, Bachmann was approached by Dr Andreas Gruentziga, a German doctor, who invented the angioplasty method using a balloon-catheter. Dr Gruentzig recommended him to undergo the surgery though it was not tested till then. "I knew it would be a breakthrough in medical history when he was talking to me about the method. He was a genius. I was sure that the surgery would be a success and happy that there would not be any post-operative complications," said Bachmann.

Quizzed whether his family was skeptical about going in for an untested method of surgery, he said, "They might have been skeptical, but I had no time to tell that I was going in for this method. I consider myself a brave person and Dr Gruentzig told me that there was a surgical team ready to step in at any moment, if something went wrong."

"He is like a god to me. He gave me a second life," he said. Dr Gruentzig kept in touch with me over telephone or through telegrams every anniversary of the surgery till his demise in a plane crash in 1985, he said.

According to Bachmann, he didn't face any problems for many years after the surgery till 2002 when another lesion was found. However, doctors observed that the original balloon catheter was still intact. Today, Bachmann is proud of being part of such a landmark treatment in the history of medicine and enjoying a retired life with a lot of activities like Nordic walking and gardening. "People need to have positive attitude even if it's a heart disease," he added.

Heading: Grandparents Day celebrated - Indian Express
Content:
A senior assistant of the Reserve Bank of India was sentenced to 6 months simple imprisonment by the Dadar metropolitan magistrate court last week in a cheque bounce case. The court also imposed a fine of Rs 1.3 lakh on him.

According to complainant Pramila Jaganath Malve, her husband Jaganath had given the accused, Sayer Lobo, a loan of Rs 1.5 lakh for purchasing property in 2001. Lobo, in return, gave a cheque dated December 14, 2001 of Karad Janta Sahakari Bank limited, Parel, to Jaganath. However, the cheque was dishonoured when Jaganath deposited it in the bank. Following which Jaganath sent a notice to Lobo which proved to be a futile. Malve then moved the court.

During the trial, Malve passed away. He had given the power of attorney to his wife Pramila who then became the complainant in the case. In between, Lobo made part payments amounting to Rs 85,000 to Pramila. The complainant's lawyer, Usha Dedhia, argued in court that the part payments made by the accused proves his guilt.

However, the defence said that the cheque was given to Jaganath as a security towards the payment of the loan. This argument was not accepted by the court and 7th metropolitan magistrate G O Agrawal who convicted Lobo under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.

The court in its judgment said that since the accused withheld the amount for a considerable period, the Malve family could not earn on it and thus directed Lobo to pay them a compensation for the loss.

Heading: Robbers break into trader’s house, decamp with Rs 15 lakh - Indian Express
Content: Students of the Lokhandwala Foundation School, Kandivili East, celebrated the Grandparents Day on September 25 and 26 at the school auditorium. 'Grandparents, You Add Colour To Our Lives' was the theme this year. All the presentations were based on this theme. Virendra Bhandarkar, assistant director of the Sports Authority of India, was the chief guest. The children welcomed their grandparents with writings, posters, pictures quotations and  painted messages.

Heading: A tale of three cities - Indian Express
Content:
Some unidentified persons broke into a cloth merchant's house at Lokhandwala on Saturday afternoon and decamped with cash amounting to Rs 15 lakh and gold jewellery worth Rs 2,50,000, said the police.

According to the Oshiwara police, the complainant, one Mohammad Rafique Ibrahim Modak (40), is a businessman and resides with his family at Sundarvan Complex near Lokhandwala Road in Andheri.

"On Saturday afternoon, Modak had gone to visit his aunt at Bandra. When he returned at night, he discovered that the latch of his door had been broken. He also found the door of the cupboard open. After checking the cupboard, he realised that valuables, including jewellery and cash kept inside the cup-board were missing," said Police Inspector Dattatray Sankhe of the Oshiwara police station.

Though there were security guards at the building, they claimed that they didn't find any strangers entering the building premises on the Saturday afternoon, said Dattatray Sankhe.

"This is unlikely as the burglary took place on Saturday afternoon. We have questioned the security staff at the building. Further investiogation is on," he added.

Heading: Musing on museums - Indian Express
Content:
Three women artists play raconteurs with art, at their solo shows across the city

Telling stories of cities imagined and real, capturing a personal moment or commenting on larger political issues, it is the week for solo shows by women artists. In keeping with the same, the city is hosting three blockbuster shows. A good blend of message and medium, the works are by Mumbai based Shilpa Gupta, Delhi based Vibha Galhotra, and Bangalore based Minam Apang.

Apang has dug into local stories and myths form North-Eastern cities. Retold by Verrier Elwin, they create a world of fantastical beings rendered in her signature style which is graphic and linear. She renders her stories on paper with spontaneity and pizzazz.

Galhotra creates imaginary landscapes of images inspired by the metropolitan, capturing teeming slums, high-rise buildings and the tangled wires of electric poles. Gupta is showcasing works from over a year-and-half. Sound, light and image installations capture her personal and political concerns.

Apang, who is showing at the Chatterjee and Lal Gallery near Radio Club, is revisiting her childhood through this body of works. "I was not brought up in the North-East. In fact, I went to a convent school in Mussoorie where we were taught sacrificing animals was a pagan practice. It was in direct contrast with the practices back home. I needed to rediscover these old stories and reconnect with my native land which is why I chose to work on the story of the War with the Stars. What I like about this narrative is that it's open-ended and can have a number of readings," says Apang, who makes it clear that a political reading was not intended in the work.

Gupta, on the other hand is explicitly political, her latest sound installation, Tryst with Destiny is a singing microphone that has a recording of Nehru's speech on the day of Independence. This work is off set by a light piece that spells out the words, Blind stars, Stars blind. These works were shown at Bodhi, Berlin and now travel to Mumbai to be shown at Bodhi Gallery in Kala Ghoda and Bodhi Space at Orange Gate, from October 11 to 31.

"I am also showing two shadow play pieces that are interactive. Personal photographs of children who cover each others eyes, ears and mouths in a hear-no-evil-speak-no-evil gesture. The overarching theme of the show is the coalescing of the personal and political," says Gupta, who's work also comments on the proliferation of electronic gadgets and the unending crowds of Mumbai.

Crowds are something that interests Galhotra as well. Her canvases speak of the clash of masses of humanity with teeming concrete structures. Mannequin-guards dressed in fatigues that are covered with images of these structures appear to patrol the gallery space while gold lettered signs caution the viewer of Work in progress. "I was inspired by the upheaval of construction in Delhi—the Master Plan 2010—but what you see is generic cities, my comment is on environmental degradation and the costs future generations pay in the bargain," says Galhotra whose show at Project 88, Colaba, is on till October 18.

Heading: What is Fluxus? - Indian Express
Content:
Tina Ambani's appointment as international trustee of the Peabody Essex museum comes at a time when Indian contemporary art has already come into its own internationally. Her appointment (whatever the reasons behind it) can however be viewed as an additional marker, one that might just ensure that the spotlight remains on the stars of Indian contemporary art.

April 2009-April 2010 will see the Museum host an exhibition titled, Trans-fusion; India's Artists Mine Their Traditions, which will feature works from the well-known Chester and Davida Herwitz Collection. We are told that, "Through the juxtaposition of more than 36 traditional and modern Indian artworks, this exhibition examines the manner in which Post-Independence artists negotiate the contemporary art world's vernacular while maintaining strong ties to their aesthetic traditions."

While both announcements are laudable in their own right, one can't help but wonder why Indian art patrons don't take as much interest in India's own museums and public galleries. Museums across the country, without exception, continue to remain in a state of abject neglect. We all know that precious objects and documents continue to languish in badly managed spaces which are in dire need of trained staff, proper lighting, temperature control systems and documentation.

Yes, the Prince of Wales Museum (or whatever its new nomenclature) and the Bhau Daji Lad museum in Mumbai have got together their respective acts to a certain degree, thanks to corporate support and the untiring efforts of leading conservationists. But I have it on record from a foreign visitor—he recently visited both museums—that the fabulously produced catalogs have fallen pray to moisture and the Mumbai monsoon, and clerks have actually to be jostled if one wants to buy a book or a souvenir.

Has anybody ever seen that happen at the Peabody or the MoMA? The point is that quality restoration and preservation efforts need to be supported by well thought-out marketing strategies and qualified curators, support staff and informed docents. Visitors from all over the world can be heard complaining about the ill-trained guide at a private museum in Ahmedabad. Sadly, the lasting impression is that of the surly staffer and not the fabulous exhibits.

And then there is the continuing saga of Mumbai's very own National Gallery of Modern Art which is run by remote control in autocratic fashion by the inimitable Rajeev Lochan who claims to monitor it from New Delhi. The director recently cut a rather sorry figure at the India Art Summit, as he bumbled on and on about all his various difficulties and the absence of budgets for his own foreign travel! The fact is that several international curators and critics who have had to beg for an audience with him have returned frustrated. In the process art audiences have missed out on some stellar exhibitions.

So, in reality, despite the fact that we chirp on about our cool cultural climate and continue to tot up sparkling results at international auctions, the state of art infrastructure in our country is in a pathetic state. Patronage and CSR on home soil, anyone?

(The columnist is an independent art consultant and writer.)

Heading: Culture vulture - Indian Express
Content:
Recently at the opening of a show conceptualised by Gitanjali Dang, a friend came across the word Fluxus, and wanted to know what it meant. Clearly she hadn't caught the exhibition at NGMA dedicated to the movement, which threw light on why a group of artists were choosing to make anti art.

For those who missed the show, Fluxus means 'flow' in Latin and it refers to merging of various disciplines; music, art and theatre, for the purpose of creating a do-it-yourself aesthetic. The origins of the movement lie in some experiments conducted by composer John Cage with atonal music; works such as 4'33" challenged the notion of harmony and fixed time signatures in art. These experiments went on to influence artists like George Maciunas who went on to organise the first Fluxus event in 1961. The movement that was loosely based on Dadaist principals of challenging establishment, it came to be known as Neo-Dadaism. Artists like Dick Higgins and Jackson Mac Low, were already practicing a kind of Fluxus with little or no knowledge of music. The idea that drove many of these artists was the element of chance for making art and music and a self driven funding for publishing under the name of the Something Else Press, which furthered the manifesto and cause of Fluxus. The movement grew to encapsulate many other disciplines like New Media art and by extension artists like Nam Jun Paik who practiced video art, were also part of the Fluxus movement. The group expanded to include George Brecht who wrote music scores that were used in art scripts and Joseph Beuys whose groundbreaking performances like How to Explain Pictures to a Dead Hare were crucial to the Fluxus movement. It represented social values and in a way critiqued society.

The Fluxus group shifted the emphasis from what an artist makes to the artist's personality, actions, and opinions and this was the basis for many art movements around the world, including the Gutai group in Japan.

(Demystify art, e-mail georgina.maddox@expressindia.com)

Heading: Enterprising spirit - Indian Express
Content:
Figuring location

Three young and ambitious artists try out different experiences, realities and materials of production. They've come up with a show that comments on their diverse locations and their influence on their art. Haraprasad Tripathy, though born in Odisha (Orissa), has been trained at Santiniketan and Baroda much of his life and art reflects those realities. Susant Panda is from a semi-urban, south Odisha town Hinjilicut and Ramakanta Samantaray is from seaside rural eastern village Masakani. Both Samantaray and Panda received their art schooling from B K College of Art and Craft, in Bhubaneswar and Khalikote Government College. All three now live and practice in Baroda. One would respect them for locating their intellectual and creative identities. This is also reflected in all their paintings which mull over urban disturbances. The intellectual and symbolic connotation being the place of violence and power in human world and nature; how violence, domination, power of various kinds such as political, economic, social and personal some times miraculously co exist both in human and the animal world.

At India Fine Art, Tardeo, till October 19, from 10 am to 6 pm

Maksed man

Deepak Bathija is inspired by African masks, and he lionises the art form through his paintings. The self-taught painter finds time to paint on weekends. He runs a boutique for clothes and accessories when he's not doing that. The dramatic and powerful forms have been captured by Bathija in bold brushstrokes in oil on canvas. The artist believes that his art will create an awareness of the great tribal art of Africa.

At Gallery Entrance, Army Navy Building,

Kala Ghoda, till October 17

Charcoal musings

Ajay De began his career rather unconventionally, eschewing colour and working on charcoal to convey his experiences on to canvas. His paintings are mostly shaped by his childhood memories. As an introvert, he often found himself at a loss for words, until he discovered the joy of putting pencil to paper to draw and express his feelings.

At Gallery Art and Soul, Worli, till October 8

Heading: Resurrecting the Mughals - Indian Express
Content:
Youth expert Rashmi Bansal talks about her book and entrepreneurship in India

When you graduate from the Indian Institute of Management -Ahmedabad (IIM-A), the world is your oyster. Each year, during the placement season, newspapers carry reports about the astronomical salaries offered to fresh graduates by companies from all over the world. But there are some who think out of the box. In IIM lingo, they're called OoPs - opting out of placement. And it is this brave tribe, which scorns the lure of money and goes for entrepreneurship, which inspired Rashmi Bansal's book Stay Hungry, Stay Foolish.

Bansal says, "I wrote this book in the hope that it would inspire people to think differently and to look at entrepreneurship as a possible career. The people in this book became entrepreneurs despite their MBAs, not because of them." The 37-year-old, herself an IIM-A alumnus, has her finger firmly on the pulse of the youth of the country. She's the co-founder and editor of Just Another Magazine or JAM and runs the popular blog Youthcurry. The idea for the book came from IIM-A professor, Rakesh Basant and the Centre for Innovation, Incubation and Entrepreneurship at the institute, but it was Bansal who realised that she should be the one to write it. "I wrote the book like someone who was looking for the holy grail of entrepreneurship," she says.

The book, whose title is inspired by Apple CEO Steve Jobs' commencement address to the 2005 graduates of Stanford, is not your typical management bible. "There are no management case studies or pie charts here," Bansal says, "It's more about the personal journeys of the entrepreneurs. While each story is different, they have some things like patience, courage and passion, in common."

The book's Mumbai launch on October 2 at Crossword bookstore, Kemp's Corner, was attended by the author herself and by four of the people featured in the book - Anand Halve, Ashank Desai, Cyrus Driver and Deepta Rangarajan. Desai, founder and ex-chairman of Mastek, one of the top 20 software companies in India, believes that there is no better time to be an entrepreneur in India. "When we started out, we didn't have a computer for four years and we used the neighbouring shopkeeper's phone," he says, outlining the difficulties Mastek faced in its initial years. Driver, CEO of Calorie Care, a health food delivery service, agrees. "But," he warns, "You should always have a backup plan, even if you decide to set out on your own. Much entrepreneurship never sees the light of day."

Rangarajan, co-founder of IRIS Business Services, describing herself as an accidental entrepreneur, says, "You just know when the time is right to venture out on your own." Halve, co-founder of Chlorophyll Brand and Communications, added to it by saying, "The right time is when the disease of entrepreneurship has got to the point where you can't help but do it."

Heading: Track Travel - Indian Express
Content:
Alpana Gujral walks into the Sea Lounge at the Taj Mahal Palace and Tower looking like the very embodiment of style. Dressed simply but elegantly in pastel shades and decked out in jewellery of her own design, the renowned jeweller makes a stunning picture, just like her one-of-a-kind pieces. She will be showing her latest collection, The Enchanted Garden, at the hotel on October 7 and 8.

The line is inspired by the perfection and symmetry of medieval Mughal gardens. "The theme allowed me to play with different forms and colours," she explains, "The flowers, animals, trees - they all go well with the feminine form and add romance to the pieces."

Gujral has a very simple work philosophy, she informs us. "I believe that there should be an emotional connection between the jewellery and the wearer. You should feel pleasure when you wear a piece. It shouldn't just be for its monetary value. In fact, I strongly believe that jewellery should be more than just an investment."

Gujral's designs are certainly more than that. Exquisitely imagined and realised, her work finds its inspiration in jewellery of the Mughal era. "I think the Mughal age was the height of jewellery design in India - the jadau technique, the enamelling at the back. There's a saying about ornaments from that time - the front of the piece is for the visual pleasure of the person standing in front of you and the decoration at the back is for the soul."

The designer believes that accessories have come of age in India. "In the last few years, jewellery as an accessory has become an important part of everyone's attire," she explains, "This is more so, because costume jewellery is widely available, so everyone can now afford to splurge more on them." Do her outfits revolve around jewellery or vice versa? She laughs and says, "I always co ordinate my clothes to match my jewellery, not the other way round." And what is her opinion on India's legendary obsession with gold? "I completely agree that gold is beautiful," she says, "It's such a warm metal and so malleable. It can take any form."

About her working style, Gujral says, there is no method to her madness. "It is very difficult to describe my style. There is no pattern that I follow. I get an idea and I execute it. But there are days when I have a mental block and then it gets very frustrating. But that is all part of the creative process. I've learnt to be patient with it," she smiles.

Heading: A Slice of The Sunshine State - Indian Express
Content:
This photographer-filmmaker has his pulse on the lifeline of the country, the Indian Railways

Thirty years ago, when UK-based documentary filmmaker Gerry Troyna (60) came to India to make a film on the Indian Railway, he never thought that his romance with the railway would last three long decades.

Since then, Troyna has made several films on railway not only in India, but also about routes joining various destinations across the globe.

Still, his love for the Indian Railways, is special. "The Indian Railways is all about energy and life. It is about a saga that speaks of economic, social and political development of the country," says Troyna, whose photographic portraits of hundreds of people associated with the Indian Railways was on show at a unique exhibition at the Piramal Gallery at the National Centre for Performing Arts (NCPA) last week. The exhibition included portraits of people Troyna had been in contact with over a 30-year period. From a coolie to a senior Indian Railway and Traffic Service (IRTS) officer, from a rag-picker to a motorman, the faces at the exhibition were collectively the human side of a great system that transports millions of people everyday.

Incidentally, Troyna is still in touch with most of those who posed for him. "You can't alienate these people from the railways. They are an integral part of the system and without the co-ordination of all these people, the railway would not function smoothly," he says.

Having made several films on the Indian Railways including a series titled 'The Great Railway Journeys: India, from East to West' and another one called 'Great Little Railway Journey' and also a two-part series on 'Monsoon Railway', the film-maker says Indian audiences are still to adapt to documentaries. "The television channels in India give very little space to documentary films," he adds. In 2006, Troyna was again asked to make a three-part film titled 'Bombay Railway: Dreams and Pressures' "We made two documentaries on the city's railway lines. I couldn't complete the third since I suffered a heart attack," he says, somewhat dejectedly.

But that experience showed him the spirit of people who battle it out everyday in the local trains. "I'm really amazed with the way common people commute in a transport system that is so very crowded. Still, when you look at it, you understand why it is known as the lifeline of the city," he says.

"Gerry's work reaffirms the fact that Indian Railway is one of the great railway systems in the world. It also brings out many interesting facts of the railway system from a foreigner's point of view," says Sriniwas Mudgerikar of the Central Railway.

Troyna's plate, meanwhile, remains full. Among the films in the pipeline is on India's mountain trains, a work in progress.

Heading: A special life - Indian Express
Content:
From football to food, everything that's quintessentially Goan will be on show at Mumbai venues all this month

This year, the month of October has an extra dash of the festive, thanks to a 'Goan Fiesta', a month-long promotional event by Goa Tourism to display the art and culture of the sunshine state.

Part of the 'Explore the Incredible States' programme of the India Tourism Mumbai office, Goan Fiesta promotes art, culture and tourism of the states in the Western Region (Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Chhatisgarh). And, true to Goan tradition, the first day of the fest saw a colourful carnival float parade at Kala Ghoda on Sunday. Sujata Thakur, regional director (western and central region), Indiatourism said: "The Goan Fiesta has been designed in a way that will help Mumbaikars visiting Goa live the true

Goan style by offering glimpses of the state."

Apart from Goan food and jazz festivals and Konkani plays, the fest will also host a 'veteran football match' between former players who have represented the state of Goa and renowned football stars from Mumbai on Monday at the Cross Maidan.

Elvis Gomes, director of tourism and managing director, Goa Tourism Development Corporation (GTDC), said: "Tourism being the backbone of the Goan economy, we want to ensure that Goa provides the best holidays to its tourists. In the recent past, there have been a number of misconceptions regarding safety. We want our visitors to know that Goa is a safe and vibrant holiday destination." Lyndon Monteiro, vice-chairman of GTDC, said: "Government of Goa has started a number of programmes to ensure safety of tourists like the integrated bit safety management scheme introduced for the first time ever in India, 24-hour surveillance on beaches, development of basic infrastructure, etc. We want more and more tourists to visit Goa."

Also present at the inauguration was actress Varsha Usgaonkar, a Goan herself.

'Explore the Incredible States' was started to 'augment the awareness of the culture and traditions of the different states to Mumbaikars'. The fest concludes on October 30.

Heading: ‘Just like realty and gold, investment in art is a wise option’ - Indian Express
Content:
Having dedicated nearly three decades to understanding and helping families cope with special children, Parul Shroff says the differently-abled are just as able

On hearing about special children ¿ physically or mentally challenged or suffering from debilitating conditions like Cerebral Palsy ¿ the image of Forest Gump breaking his crutches or that of Darsheel Safary creating his masterpiece painting is what comes to mind, but at Ghatkopar's Smt Rukshmaniben Amritlal Sheth Shartul Gurukul, special children are simply that — built differently and talented in ways most don't understand.

A school for special children run by the Shartul Foundation, the Shartul Gurukul is where 60 special children from all corners of Mumbai and from every socio-economic background come every day. Most special here is the school's belief: That it's not just the child who requires special treatment but parents and family members as well. "Ultimately, both the parents and children should not be afraid of going out in public because of the child's limitations. So even parents need to be counselled," says Parul Shroff, founding member of the Shartul Foundation.

It was in year 1982 that Shroff, 58, along with Ela Mehta, started a toy library for special children. They started with just four members.

Initially, all they got was a cupboard to keep their toys from the Children Orthopaedic Centre in Mahalaxmi. "In those times such therapeutic and educational toys were not available in India and therefore we had to ask friends and relatives to bring them from abroad," said the visibly relaxed Shroff who herself started her career as a therapist and has been supporting the cause of special children with orthopaedic deficiencies for the past 28 years.

Another aspect of her foundation is the Shartul Club that was established in 1993. "The club was started for the special children and we meet on the second Sunday of every month. The aim is to engage children in activities so that they do not hesitate to come out in public. This leads to emotional security and raises their self-esteem and confidence, turning disabled into differently abled," she says.

The club has more than 130 members in its roll and members of the club have gone on to become lawyers, doctors and even jewellery designers.

"Ela and me had gone on a trip to Europe and it was on that tour that we decided to do something concrete for spastic children and that is how we started the toy library," says Shroff, commenting on their initial days. An exhibition and fair organised by the foundation came to an end last week, where the children's art works were displayed and parents and children mingled, sharing challenges and homegrown strategies to deal with special needs.

But Shroff's real feat comes out when she talks about this special couple who are also members of their group. "Both, the husband and the wife, are special but today they lead a very respectable life. Today the husband earns more than Rs 30,000 a month and they even have a daughter who is perfectly healthy."

Heading: Rs 1.30 lakh stolen from Miller Ganj - Indian Express
Content:
From Mumbai to Ludhiana and from diamonds to selling art, Sukhvir Singh has done it all. Owner of the lone art gallery in the city — Artmosphere, Newsline catches up with him to know more about art as a possible investment.

Ques There are many places in the city that sell paintings. How is Artmosphere different?

People have to learn the difference between an art gallery and a shop selling art wares. An art gallery is a place where one can walk-in to enjoy pieces of art while shops are only where products are sold. We do not simply collect pieces from painters and put them up to sell. We have a curator who is a part of this art world and knows how to guide you around.

Ques How is art as an investment?

I am a diamond merchant. People come to me to seek advise on how and how much to invest in jewellery. Everyone wants to see his or her money grow by leaps and bounds. I suggest investment in arts is a good option. We all read news how paintings are being sold in crores and while these may seem to be out of our bounds at present but then there are many artists who may be sold in thousands or a few lakhs now but a decade later will rake in huge sums. It is these artists that we need to invest in. Remember, to begin with even M F Hussain and Anjali Ela Menon sold for a few thousands and today their works command crores.

Ques How can an investor decide what to buy?

It is here that the art galleries come into picture. They not only help an investor buy an original piece of art but also guide whereto put the money. On his own part the investor should see that the artist that he investing on is consistent in producing his work and more over with each work he is maturing. Consistency is very important. Galleries may have their own favourites but on the whole the art scene has a few geniuses and they are known to all.

Ques Any names that you would like to suggest?

There is a batch of young artists to keep an eye on. The works are available at easy prices now but these artists will go places. Anirbaan Das Gupta is just 24 years old, Hemant Sathe and his batch, Julius Macwaha, Ram Das Tarke are some other names that are heating up the art scene. I may have missed a few but regular visitors to the art galleries are well informed.

Ques How does the money grow in art as compared to land and gold?

It is almost on a par if not better. See gold worth Rs 30,000 today will fetch Rs 30 lakh after a decade. It may touch a few lakhs mark. Property can do that but then fluctuation in property prices is very volatile. Amidst all this art is one thing which can really grow. An artist's work that you pick up today for Rs 4 lakh or Rs 5 lakh today can fetch you Rs 40 to Rs 50 lakh bracket in the next ten years.

Heading: PAUTA stands up for Dr Brar - Indian Express
Content:
Some unidentified persons allegedly stole Rs 1.30 lakh from a scooter, in Miller Ganj area today.

Kuldeep Singh, an employee of JGN Flour Mills, had withdrawn the money from a private multinational bank and kept it in his scooter.

Then he went to another bank leaving the money in the scooter. When he came back after sometime, he found the lock of dickey broke open and the money was stolen.

With nearly 50 branches and ATMs of different banks and financial institutions situated in Miller Ganj, the area is fast becoming a favourite hunting ground for robbers and snatchers.

The number of snatching and theft incidents has recorded an unprecedented rise in the recent months.

Recently, some unidentified robbers had snatched money on gunpoint from an employee of a private firm.

Earlier on June 29, some unidentified thieves burgled Rs 30,000 by breaking open the trunk of a scooter of one Mandeep Singh, an employee of New Era Enterprisis.

In another incident, some robbers had snatched the luxury car of a local businessman in the Miller Ganj area when he was returning home after dropping his relatives at the local railway station.

Sandeep Sharma, DSP Control Room and PCR, said that the recently introduced CCTV mobile vans will help in tracking the culprits.

Heading: 70-feet tall Ravana all set to light up city - Indian Express
Content:
The Punjab Agricultural University Teachers' Association (PAUTA) seems to have already announced its verdict on the sexual harassment case in which Director Students Welfare Dr Dulcha Singh Brar is facing an inquiry.

The association is offering unflinching support to Dr Brar giving it a 'same fraternity' hue.

It has been learnt that last week, a delegation of teachers from PAUTA had met Dr Dulcha Singh Brar to express their solidarity with him.

The PAUTA delegation also met V-C Dr Manjit Singh Kang and took up the matter with him. Dr Mukesh Siag, general secretary, PAUTA, said, "Dr Brar had come to us and spoken to us about the matter. We met the V-C to know about the issue." When asked what are the issues that PAUTA has discussed with the V-C, Dr Siag said, "We just wanted to know what the matter is. We did point it out to the V-C that by withdrawing the charge of girls' hostel from Dr Brar even before the completion of the probe was unjustified. This was like awarding punishment to him. Dr Kang told us that this is an administrative change."

Dr Siag further added, "We just want the inquiry to be completed at the earliest so that the truth is out soon."

Maintaining the same rhetoric, Harbans Singh Mundi, president, PAU Non-Teaching Employees, added, "The complainant has not approached us to seek any support. But then we would rather not support anyone without knowing the truth. We are waiting for the probe to get over."

Much action is expected tomorrow when the university reopens after almost a weeklong holidays.

Heading: Children’s eyes are rivetted on Ramlila - Indian Express
Content:
Come October and there are festivities all around. This year it is Dussehra (October 9) that will lend a punch to the upbeat mood. The effigies of Ravana, Kumbhkaran and Meghnath are being prepared on a warfooting at the historical Daresi ground in the city.

The ground is full of commotion. Some are busy in stitching black dresses while others are busy painting masks. This year, the effigy of Ravana will be 70-feet high. The effigies of Meghnathh and Kumbhakaran are more than 60-feet high.

At Daresi, all the three effigies will not be burnt the same day. On October 7, Kumbhakarna will be set on fire; October 8 has been reserved for Meghnath, while Ravana will hit the flames on October 9.

A worker who is preparing these effigies said, "The crackers will be filled in the on the same day."

Munshi Rehman, a tailor, said, "It has been more than a week that I have been stitching the huge dress of Ravana. There are more than 15 places where Dussehra will be celebrated in and around the city. All the dresses will be sewn by me."

A 35-feet effigy of Ravana is being prepared for the Basant Avenue Dussehra Committee. Subhash Medh, an office-bearer of the committee, said, "Some Muradabad-based artists are preparing it. We hope to see a huge rush this year."

The effigy of Ravana will be 40-feet high at Kitchlu Nagar. Parkash Chopra, General Secretary, Dussehra Committee of Kichlu Nagar, said, "After burning the effigies of Meghnath, Kumbhkaran and Ravana, we will have special fireworks for 45 minutes."

Heading: Experts share important facts about heart ailments - Indian Express
Content:
Ram Lila is being staged by different theatrical groups in the city. Everyone of them is trying its level best to convey the message of the Ramayana. And majority of viewers who keenly observe each and every character as well scene are children.

Interestingly, children are preferring regular Ramlila over TV channels this time. Sarika Sharma, a Vth class student, said, "I have read the story of Ramayana and have also watched a movie based on it. But I love to watch these characters in colourful attires. I am amazed to see how quickly Sahrupnakha changes herself from a vamp to a beautiful lady."

Not only characters but the light-and-sound effects have also added to the attraction for the viewers. Rahul Khanna, an VIIIth standard boy, said, "The characters I like most in Ramlila are Laxman and Ravana. The way Ravana laughs loudly and speaks his dialogues is very good."

It has been observed that children, who visit Dusshehra mela and watch Ramlila, love to do the sword acts and while doing them they repeat the same dialogues which they hear at Ramlila. Suman Kanta, a home maker, said, "I could not help laughing when my six-year-old son stood in front of the mirror, and said, "Hum Ravan hain, Yamraj bhi hamse darta hai. To yeh vanar mera kya bigad lenge."

The favourite characters which children love to see are Hanuman and Ravana. While watching Ramlila, children come up with many queries. Rakesh Kumar, whose son watches Ramila, keenly said, "Today my son asked as to why the man who played Ram's role yesterday has become Laxman today? Then I made him understand that he might have some other work to do."

Heading: Ludhiana girls win soccer tournament - Indian Express
Content:
More than 90 physicians of Ludhiana attended the Continuing Medical Education (CME) programme held under the aegis of Punjab Medical Council, Mohali, on "Cardiology update 2008" in the city on Saturday. This was stated by Dr Devinderjit S Walia, president of the Physicians Association, Ludhiana, which organised the event today.

Dr K.K. Talwar, Director Prof and Head of Cardiology, PGI, Dr Ajay Bahl, Assistant Prof, PGI, Dr Manmohan Singh, a renowned cardiologist and president of Punjab Medical Council, Mohali, Dr S.B. Khurana, former principal and head of the Department of Medicine DMC, Ludhiana and Dr Gurpreet S. Wander, chief cardiologist of Hero-DMC Heart Institute, participated in the panel discussion session with the delegates.

Dr K.K Talwar stressed on the need for early diagnosis of heart attack and the importance of clinical judgement in differentiating a heart attack from non-cardiac chest pain. Importance of giving early thrombolytic therapy during the first three hours and PCI after three hours of the occurence of the chest pain was stressed. Importance of Doppler evaluation for wall motion abnormalities and Troponin - T quantification was also stressed.

Speaking on the acute and chronic management of heart failure, Dr Ajay Behal stressed on the need for patients to take regular medicines so that they are symptomatically better. Apart from the usual causes of cardiac failure, the need for endomyocardial biopsy was also stressed for the proper diagnosis of some patients of heart failure.

Dr Manmohan Singh talked about the importance of need of when and when not to treat diastolic heart failure.

Dr Vikas Loomba , secretary of the association, said that this event was a total success as it clarified a lot of doubts and misgivings about the treatment and management of acute coronary syndrome and heart failure.

Dr L.S. Chawla, former vice-chancellor of Baba Farid University and principal and head of medicine, DMC, described Dr Talwar as the most successful directors of PGI.
